headline: Climate deals, forgotten grasslands and the carbon in every breath
teaser: Can an energy crisis speed up climate action? Was Europe ever really a land of endless forest? And should we worry about the CO2 we breathe out?

articles.title: Antalya's Balancing Act: Can Climate Talks Survive an Energy Crisis?
articles.dek: COP31 opens in Türkiye as war drives up energy prices. Will the crisis push countries toward clean power, or away from their climate promises?
paras: On Monday, November 9, delegates from nearly 200 countries will gather in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for COP31, the United Nations’ annual climate summit. For almost two weeks, until November 20, ministers, diplomats, scientists and activists will argue over how quickly the world should cut the greenhouse gases that are warming the planet. More than 100,000 people are expected to attend, and dozens of world leaders are scheduled to speak at a leaders’ summit on November 11 and 12. Yet many observers believe this year’s talks will be among the most difficult in recent memory.

Part of the difficulty is visible in the summit’s unusual structure. Under UN rules dating back to 1992, Türkiye and Australia belong to the same regional group, and both wanted to host the 2026 conference. Because the climate treaty has no mechanism for settling competing bids, the two countries reached a compromise at last year’s summit in Brazil: Türkiye hosts the event and leads a programme of voluntary “action” commitments, while Australia, represented by its climate minister Chris Bowen, chairs the formal negotiations. Supporters say the arrangement shows that rivals can cooperate; critics worry that divided leadership may blur responsibility if the talks stall.

The scientific backdrop is sobering. According to a recent report from the UN Environment Programme, even if every country fully implemented its current pledges, the world would still be on course for about 2.6°C of warming this century — far above the 1.5°C goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Scientists now accept that the 1.5°C threshold will be crossed, at least temporarily, and global carbon emissions have yet to peak. A strong El Niño, a natural climate pattern that releases heat from the Pacific Ocean, could make 2026 or 2027 the hottest year on record.

Against this background, the co-hosts have chosen a practical centrepiece: electrification. Today, electricity supplies only about 20 percent of the world’s final energy demand; the rest comes mostly from burning fuels directly in cars, furnaces and boilers. Türkiye and Australia want countries to commit to raising that share to 35 percent by 2035. The logic is that electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial machines can run on power from solar and wind farms, whereas a petrol engine cannot. “I would like to see a strong outcome on electrification,” Bowen has said.

Optimists believe the timing is surprisingly favourable. An energy crisis linked to war in the Middle East has pushed up oil and gas prices, reminding importing countries how vulnerable they are to distant conflicts. Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, has argued that this pressure could produce a “climate action comeback,” because producing electricity at home from sunlight and wind is both cleaner and more secure. “I have rarely seen the energy security policy objectives and the climate objectives so closely aligned,” he said.

Skeptics, however, point to contradictions closer to home. Coal remains Türkiye’s largest source of electricity, and its national climate plan allows emissions to keep rising rather than falling, although the government did cancel the expansion of a major coal plant in July. Australia, one of the world’s largest exporters of coal and gas, has declined to set an end date for coal. Campaigners also note that the 2023 summit in Dubai promised a “transition away from fossil fuels,” yet last year’s final agreement in Brazil did not explicitly mention them. To these critics, a focus on electrification risks becoming a comfortable way to avoid the harder question of when fossil fuels will actually be abandoned.

Money is a third fault line. African negotiators want wealthy nations to triple funding for adaptation — the sea walls, drought-resistant crops and early-warning systems that help communities cope with the warming that is already unavoidable. Developed countries, facing high energy bills and tight budgets of their own, have been reluctant to promise more. Meanwhile, the United States government is not taking part in the negotiations at all, sending only a delegation from Congress, which weakens the pressure on other large emitters.

Because every COP decision requires consensus among nearly 200 governments, a single country can block an agreement. Bowen himself has admitted that reaching a deal “will not be easy.” Whether Antalya succeeds may therefore depend less on dramatic announcements than on measurable commitments, such as electrification targets, that countries can be held to. In my view, a modest but specific agreement would be worth more than another ambitious promise that is quietly forgotten; the real test of COP31 will come not on November 20, but in the years that follow.

keySentences.text: Yet many observers believe this year’s talks will be among the most difficult in recent memory.
keySentences.note: “Yet” turns from the facts of the summit to the article’s central claim: these talks will be hard. Main-idea questions often hide behind contrast words.
A short topic sentence that sets the tone; every detail that follows (2.6°C, emissions not peaking, El Niño) supports it.

keySentences.text: Optimists believe the timing is surprisingly favourable.
keySentences.note: Introduces the first side of the debate. Track who holds each view: optimists here, skeptics in paragraph 6.

keySentences.text: To these critics, a focus on electrification risks becoming a comfortable way to avoid the harder question of when fossil fuels will actually be abandoned.
keySentences.note: The critics’ main argument. “Risks becoming” is hedged language: it is a warning, not a fact.

keySentences.text: Because every COP decision requires consensus among nearly 200 governments, a single country can block an agreement.
keySentences.note: A clear cause-and-effect structure (“Because …, …”) that TOEFL often tests in factual and inference questions.

keySentences.text: In my view, a modest but specific agreement would be worth more than another ambitious promise that is quietly forgotten; the real test of COP31 will come not on November 20, but in the years that follow.
keySentences.note: “In my view” signals the author’s own judgement, which differs from the reported opinions of optimists and skeptics.

speak.p: Some people believe that international meetings like COP31 are the best way to fight climate change. Others think individual countries, cities or companies can achieve more on their own. Which view do you agree with, and why? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (scale/fairness or speed) + example → reason 2 + example → one-sentence conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week, nearly 200 countries meet at COP31. Because of an energy crisis, some argue that governments should focus first on keeping energy cheap and secure, even if climate goals are delayed. Others say the crisis is exactly the reason to speed up the switch to clean electricity. What do you think governments should prioritise right now, and why? (Leo says: Families are struggling with high bills now. Governments should first protect people from rising prices, then return to climate targets when the crisis is over.) (Ana says: Solar and wind power are produced at home, so they protect countries from foreign conflicts. The crisis is a reason to move faster, not slower.)
steps: Choose a side, or a balanced position, in one sentence.
Give one reason with a concrete example (prices, jobs, energy security).
Respond to Leo or Ana: agree with part of their idea, then add something new.
Finish with a short concluding sentence.

articles.title: Was Europe Ever Really a Land of Endless Forest?
articles.dek: A major review suggests Europe’s wild landscape was a patchwork of woods and grassland kept open by giant grazers. Should we still plant dense forests everywhere?
paras: Ask many Europeans to imagine their continent before farmers arrived, and they will picture a dark, unbroken forest stretching from the Atlantic to the Urals — the kind of wilderness found in fairy tales. This image has shaped science and policy for generations. Conservationists have often treated closed-canopy forest, in which the crowns of tall trees touch and shade the ground below, as Europe’s “natural” state, and many governments still measure environmental progress by how many trees they plant. A study from Aarhus University in Denmark, published in the journal Biological Conservation and widely discussed again this week, argues that this picture is largely mistaken.

The researchers, led by doctoral researcher Szymon Czyżewski and senior author Professor Jens-Christian Svenning, reviewed evidence covering roughly the last 23 million years, from the Miocene epoch to the period just before industrialisation. Their conclusion is striking: for more than 20 million years, much of Europe was a mosaic of scattered trees, open woodland, scrub, grassland and flowering meadows. Dense, dark forests, they argue, are a relatively recent phenomenon. Importantly, the mosaic persisted not only during unusually warm or cold periods but also under temperate climates similar to today’s.

What kept the landscape open? The authors point to large plant-eating animals. Elephants, rhinoceroses, wild horses, aurochs — the giant wild ancestors of cattle — and bison browsed young trees, broke branches and trampled vegetation, creating clearings where light-loving plants could thrive. As most of these animals disappeared, first through extinction at the end of the last ice age and later through hunting and land-use change, the forces that held trees in check weakened. According to the study, much of the most recent shift has happened within the last hundred years, as traditional grazing by livestock vanished from large parts of the countryside.

The evidence comes from many sources rather than one. Traditionally, scientists reconstructed ancient vegetation mainly from fossil pollen trapped in lake sediments. The Aarhus team combined pollen with preserved plant remains, ancient charcoal, chemical isotopes in fossil teeth and bones, fossil insects such as dung beetles — a sign of large grazing herds — and environmental DNA recovered from soil. They paid special attention to the Eemian interglacial, a warm period about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago, when the climate resembled today’s but human influence was minimal.

The idea is not entirely new. Around the turn of the century, the Dutch ecologist Frans Vera proposed that grazing animals had kept Europe’s primeval landscape partly open, and his theory provoked fierce debate. Critics noted that pollen records from many sites are dominated by tree pollen, which they took as evidence of largely closed forests. Supporters of the new study argue that pollen alone can be misleading, because trees produce and spread far more pollen than many grassland plants, and that combining several independent types of evidence gives a more reliable picture.

If the authors are right, the implications for conservation are significant. Many species now associated with farmland, such as larks, jackdaws and the European hamster, may originally have evolved in open woodland shaped by wild herbivores. Planting dense forest everywhere could therefore remove the very habitats these species depend on. The researchers single out Denmark, where public subsidies support only the planting of dense forest; Svenning warned that this approach “will not only be harmful for biodiversity” but also contradicts the ecosystems in which Europe’s species evolved.

Not everyone will be persuaded. Dense forests can store large amounts of carbon, so governments trying to meet climate targets have strong reasons to favour them. Bringing back large herbivores, meanwhile, raises practical problems: bison and wild cattle need space, may damage crops and can collide with cars on busy roads. Some scientists may also question how confidently a landscape that existed millions of years ago can guide decisions about a crowded continent today.

The authors themselves do not call for recreating an ancient landscape exactly. Instead, they suggest restoring the natural processes, especially grazing, that once made Europe’s ecosystems diverse and resilient. Their study is a reminder that “natural” is not a fixed snapshot but a moving target. In my view, the strongest lesson is not that tree planting is wrong, but that conservation goals should be based on evidence rather than on a fairy-tale image of the past.

write.p: Professor: A new study suggests that Europe’s natural landscape was a mix of woods and open grassland kept open by large grazing animals such as bison. Some conservationists now want to bring large herbivores back to wild areas. Others think tree planting is simpler and better for the climate. Which approach should governments support, and why? (Sara says: Bringing back bison and wild horses restores the natural process that created Europe’s biodiversity. Planting dense forests everywhere could destroy habitats for many species.) (Tom says: Forests store carbon, and we are in a climate emergency. Large animals may damage farms and cause road accidents, so planting trees is the safer choice.)
steps: State which approach you support, or how to combine them.
Give one reason with an example (biodiversity, carbon, safety, cost).
Respond to Sara or Tom with a new point.

articles.title: Every Breath We Take: Counting the Carbon in Human Metabolism
articles.dek: Humans breathe out about two billion tonnes of CO2 a year. Is that a climate problem, or a striking number that is easy to misread?
paras: Every time you breathe out, you release a small puff of carbon dioxide, the same gas that is driving climate change when it comes from cars and power stations. One person’s breath seems trivial, but there are now more than eight billion of us. A new study led by the University of Bath in the United Kingdom, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, has attempted to calculate how much carbon dioxide all of humanity produces simply by staying alive. The answer — about two billion tonnes a year — has produced attention-grabbing headlines, but its real meaning is more subtle than they suggest.

To understand where this gas comes from, it helps to recall basic biology. Our cells release energy from food through a process called cellular respiration, in which sugars and fats react with oxygen to produce energy, water and carbon dioxide. The blood carries the carbon dioxide to the lungs, and we exhale it. The more energy a body uses — because it is larger, more active or still growing — the more carbon dioxide it generates.

The research team, led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the university’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, combined thousands of real-world measurements of people from infancy to old age with global data on population and body weight. They estimated that the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism rose from about 1.18 billion tonnes in 1985 to about 2.05 billion tonnes in 2015, an increase of 74 percent. More than 60 percent of that growth was explained by the rising number of people, rather than by each person producing much more.

Should we therefore worry about our breathing? The researchers insist that we should not. “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels,” Gonzalez said. The carbon in our food was absorbed from the atmosphere by plants only recently, usually months or a few years earlier, so exhaling it simply returns it to the air in a short, closed loop. Coal, oil and gas, by contrast, contain carbon that was locked underground for millions of years; burning them adds new carbon to the atmosphere. “We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change,” he stressed, and the team does not recommend that anyone exercise less or change their diet.

If breathing is not the problem, why count it at all? The answer lies in carbon accounting. Scientists track where carbon comes from and where it goes in order to predict how the climate will respond to different policies, and their models depend on getting every part of the carbon cycle right. According to the researchers, human metabolism is a sizeable part of that cycle, particularly in densely populated towns and cities. When sensors measure the carbon dioxide rising from a city, some of it comes from millions of exhaling residents; if that share is ignored or misjudged, estimates of emissions from traffic or heating could be distorted.

Critics of the media coverage argue that headlines such as “humans emit two billion tonnes of CO2 just by staying alive” risk confusing the public. Some readers might conclude that population growth itself is the main cause of global warming, or that cutting emissions is pointless because people must breathe. Yet the countries where populations are growing fastest generally have the lowest fossil-fuel emissions per person, while a relatively small share of wealthy consumers accounts for a large proportion of global emissions.

Others point out that the story does not end at the lungs. Although the carbon we exhale is part of a short cycle, producing our food often involves fossil fuels — in fertilisers, farm machinery, transport and refrigeration. From this perspective, diet does matter for the climate, not because of what we breathe out, but because of the energy used to grow and deliver what we eat. The study itself does not make this argument, but it highlights how closely human biology is connected to wider systems.

In my view, the Bath study is valuable precisely because its finding is so easy to misread. It shows that careful scientific accounting must include even the most ordinary activities, while reminding us that not all carbon dioxide is equal. The lesson for readers is to look beyond a striking number and ask where the carbon came from, and how long it was stored, before deciding whether it matters.

keySentences.text: The answer — about two billion tonnes a year — has produced attention-grabbing headlines, but its real meaning is more subtle than they suggest.
keySentences.note: The thesis: a big number with a subtle meaning. The rest of the article explains why the number is easy to misread.

keySentences.text: More than 60 percent of that growth was explained by the rising number of people, rather than by each person producing much more.
keySentences.note: A classic factual-question sentence: “rather than” separates the real cause from a tempting wrong one.

keySentences.text: Coal, oil and gas, by contrast, contain carbon that was locked underground for millions of years; burning them adds new carbon to the atmosphere.
keySentences.note: “By contrast” marks the key difference between breath carbon and fossil carbon — the logical heart of the article.

keySentences.text: If breathing is not the problem, why count it at all? The answer lies in carbon accounting.
keySentences.note: A rhetorical question introduces the purpose of the research. Expect a rhetorical-purpose question here.

keySentences.text: Critics of the media coverage argue that headlines such as “humans emit two billion tonnes of CO2 just by staying alive” risk confusing the public.
keySentences.note: Shows how the framing of a fact, not the fact itself, can mislead readers.

keySentences.text: In my view, the Bath study is valuable precisely because its finding is so easy to misread.
keySentences.note: The author’s judgement: the study’s value lies partly in teaching readers to think carefully about numbers.

questions.q: The word “trivial” in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
opts: related to quiz facts
harmful
invisible
insignificant
questions.why: One breath seems too small to matter, so “trivial” means insignificant.
optWhy: Another meaning trap: “trivia” means quiz-style facts, but “trivial” means unimportant.
Opposite idea: the sentence stresses that one breath seems too small to cause harm.
Detail swapped: CO2 is invisible, but that is not what “trivial” means here.
Correct. One breath seems too small to matter.

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, what was the main reason for the rise in metabolic CO2 between 1985 and 2015?
opts: People exercised much more than before.
There were many more people alive.
Average body weight roughly doubled.
Measurement methods became more accurate.
questions.evidence: More than 60 percent of that growth was explained by the rising number of people
questions.why: Most of the growth came from the rising number of people, not from each person producing much more.
optWhy: Not mentioned: exercise levels are not given as a cause.
Correct. Population growth explained more than 60 percent of the increase.
Not mentioned / too extreme: body-weight data were used, but no doubling is stated.
Detail swapped: “real-world measurements” were the method, not the cause of the rise.

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, all of the following are true about the carbon we breathe out EXCEPT:
opts: It was taken from the air by plants fairly recently.
It returns to the atmosphere in a short loop.
It had been stored underground for millions of years.
It differs from the carbon that is released when coal is burned.
questions.evidence: Coal, oil and gas, by contrast, contain carbon that was locked underground for millions of years
questions.why: Carbon stored underground for millions of years describes fossil fuels, not the carbon we exhale.
optWhy: Stated: plants absorbed it “only recently.”
Stated: exhaling returns it “in a short, closed loop.”
Correct. This describes fossil fuels, which the paragraph contrasts with breath.
Stated: Gonzalez says exhaled CO2 “is not the same as burning fossil fuels.”

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 5 about measuring emissions in cities?
opts: Ignoring human breathing could make traffic emissions appear larger.
City sensors are unable to detect any carbon dioxide from vehicles.
Human breathing produces more CO2 than road traffic in most large cities.
Cities should reduce their populations to cut their emissions.
questions.evidence: if that share is ignored or misjudged, estimates of emissions from traffic or heating could be distorted
questions.why: If breath CO2 is missed, it may be wrongly counted as coming from traffic or heating, so those estimates could be too high.
optWhy: Correct. Unaccounted breath CO2 could be wrongly assigned to traffic or heating.
Not stated: sensors measure all CO2 rising from a city, including traffic.
Too extreme / not stated: the passage calls metabolism “sizeable,” not larger than traffic.
Not stated: the passage makes no recommendation about population size.

questions.q: Why does the author explain cellular respiration in paragraph 2?
opts: To argue that active people harm the climate more than others
To show that the Bath study relied on new medical technology
To prove that exhaled carbon dioxide causes global warming
To give background on how the human body makes carbon dioxide
questions.evidence: Our cells release energy from food through a process called cellular respiration
questions.why: The paragraph begins “it helps to recall basic biology”: it provides background on where exhaled CO2 comes from.
optWhy: Not the purpose: activity raises CO2 output, but the author never says active people harm the climate.
Not mentioned: the paragraph is about biology, not research technology.
Contradicts the passage: the researchers say breathing is not driving climate change.
Correct. It explains the biological source of exhaled CO2.

questions.q: Which of the sentences below best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 7?
opts: Diet affects the climate through the energy used to produce and transport food, not through breathing.
Both breathing and the production of food have a large and similar effect on the climate.
What we breathe out matters more for the climate than how our food is grown.
People should stop eating any food that has been transported long distances.
questions.evidence: From this perspective, diet does matter for the climate, not because of what we breathe out, but because of the energy used to grow and deliver what we eat.
questions.why: The sentence contrasts two causes: diet matters because of food-production energy, not because of exhaled breath.
optWhy: Correct. Keeps the contrast “not because of … but because of …”.
Distorts the contrast: the sentence says breathing is not the reason diet matters.
Reverses the comparison: food-production energy is the important factor, not breath.
Too extreme / not stated: the sentence gives no advice about what to eat.
questions.highlight: From this perspective, diet does matter for the climate, not because of what we breathe out, but because of the energy used to grow and deliver what we eat.

write.p: Professor: A recent study found that humans breathe out about two billion tonnes of carbon dioxide each year, and some headlines presented this as a climate problem. Who has the greater responsibility for preventing misunderstandings about science: journalists who write the headlines, or readers who share them? Explain your view. (Ming says: Journalists are professionals. They should write accurate headlines, because most people only read the headline and never the full article.) (Emma says: Readers cannot blame the media for everything. Before sharing a story, everyone should read it carefully and check the facts.)
steps: Decide who carries more responsibility, or argue for sharing it.
Give a reason with an example (a viral post, a misleading number).
Respond to Ming or Emma with a new idea.
